entries.title: First Look at the Bigme B6 PRO E-Reader
entries.summary: The Bigme B6 Pro is an ultra-premium, pocket-sized 6-inch color E-Ink tablet that acts more like an Android phone than a traditional e-reader thanks to its blistering 75 FPS refresh speed, massive 8GB RAM, and built-in 4G LTE cellular calling. The post First Look at the Bigme B6 PRO E-Reader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Bigme B6 Pro is an ultra-premium, pocket-sized 6-inch color E-Ink e-reader and paper tablet running an open Android 14 operating system. Positioned as a heavily upgraded, top-tier alternative to standard compact e-readers, it differentiates itself by integrating 4G LTE cellular connectivity and exceptionally fast refresh algorithms.

The Bigme B6 Pro features a 6-inch Kaleido 3 color e-paper screen, presenting crisp monochrome text at 300 PPI and color content at 150 PPI. Boasts an industry-leading refresh rate of 75-85 FPS, drastically minimizing ghosting and enabling incredibly smooth web browsing, comic panning, and video playback.

The Bigme B6 Pro features a highly customizable 36-level adjustable dual front-light system. It utilizes white and amber LEDs on the side bezels to direct light across the screen surface, providing a glare-free, paper-like illumination that emits zero blue light and remains entirely flicker-free.

Under the hood is a MediaTek Dimensity 1080 processor, 8GB of RAM, and 256GB of internal storage. There is a MicroSD card slot capable of storing an additional 1TB. Dual-band Wi-Fi (2.4GHz / 5GHz) and Bluetooth 5.1 are available. Built-in High-Definition HIFI stereo speaker and dual-microphone array with integrated GPT AI voice transcription. It is powered by a 2,100 mAh battery.

Supports active electromagnetic resonance (EMR) stylus tracking for handwriting, sketch note-taking, and PDF document markup. Built-in local GPT artificial intelligence models capable of real-time multi-language voice transcription, text generation, document translation, and one-click meeting summaries.

Android 14 OS with full Google Play Store support to download third-party apps like Kindle, KOReader, or Libby.

entries.title: Bigme Launches New E-INK Photo Frame
entries.summary: The Bigme E-Ink Photo Frame ecosystem represents a specialized lineup of cordless digital posters that function as glare-free, paper-like displays for home decor, scheduling, and digital art. The post Bigme Launches New E-INK Photo Frame first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Bigme has launched its new line of color E-Ink digital photo frames, featuring the compact 7.3- or 7.5-inch F7 and F7 Pro models, as well as the larger 13.3-inch F13. The company hopes to compete in this space against Pocketbook Inkposter, Aluratek ePaper 13.3, Philips Tableaux series, and the Samsung Color E-Paper EMDX Series.

While Bigme is widely known for its E-Ink tablets and e-readers, their “poster” line focuses on the Bigme F7 and F7 Pro Smart Digital Color E-Ink Frames. Rather than targeting massive commercial wall space like Philips or Samsung, Bigme designs compact, premium desktop frames that function as smart digital posters, weather calendars, and memos.

The standard F7 edition features an 800 x 480-resolution panel. It operates entirely cord-free via a built-in 1,300 mAh rechargeable battery designed to last for months on a single charge. It is available starting at around $123.28 CAD.

The Bigme F7 Pro is an upgraded HD variant utilizing a higher-density E Ink Spectra display. It bumps the screen resolution to 1024 x 600 with 158 PPI for significantly sharper text rendering and better fine-grain color saturation. It retails for around $137.13 CAD on the Bigme Official Store.

The Bigme F13 is a 13.3-inch smart color E-Ink digital art and photo frame. It employs an E Ink Spectra 6 Panel. It implements E Ink’s premium Spectra 6 full-color electronic paper technology, delivering a rich, highly saturated, completely glare-free print visual. Positioned as a significantly larger, premium upgrade to Bigme’s compact 7-inch desktop models, it transitions the ecosystem from a desk trinket into a proper wall-mounted visual poster or gallery showcase. The frame officially retails on the Bigme Official Store at a promotional price of $239 USD or regularly $289 USD

entries.title: Podcast: Amazon Price Hikes, Pocketbook Q and Onyx Picco
entries.summary: In this edition of the Good e-Reader Radio Show, we talk about Kindle Price Hikes, if Ad-supported Kindles now make less sense, and the new Pocketbook Q e-reader. The post Podcast: Amazon Price Hikes, Pocketbook Q and Onyx Picco first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has raised prices on its hardware devices like Echo, Kindle, and Fire TV by up to 60% due to a global memory and storage chip shortage. Amazon stated it delayed raising prices for as long as possible before updating its product line pricing. Kindle prices have increased anywhere from $30 to $60.

The PocketBook Q is a newly announced, smartphone-sized e-reader designed specifically to curb phone distractions and promote one-handed reading. Officially introduced in August 2026, the device ditches the wide tablet format of standard e-readers for an ultra-portable, pocket-friendly design.

The BOOX Picco is a micro-sized, pocket e-reader teased by Onyx in July 2026. It initiates an entirely new ultra-portable product category for the brand called the BOOX Tile line.

entries.title: Do Ad-Supported Kindles Make Sense in 2026?
entries.summary: With basic hardware now starting at $149, saving 13% by staring at lock-screen advertisements feels less acceptable to buyers, especially when competitors like Kobo offer feature-rich alternatives. The post Do Ad-Supported Kindles Make Sense in 2026? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon is the only company in the e-reader space that charges two different prices for its models; one with advertisements and one without. The ad-supported ones cost $20 less than the ones that do not show them. If you buy or are gifted an e-reader with ads, you can pay Amazon directly to remove them at a later date. Do advertisements make sense in 2026?

Amazon recently increased prices across its e-reader lineup, raising the basic Kindle to $149 with ads and $169 without it, while the Paperwhite jumped to $199 for the ad-supported version. Paying $20 less gets you an ad-supported device, but the ads are strictly limited to the lock screen/sleep screen. They never interrupt your actual reading. Ad-supported models show sponsored screen savers and require an extra swipe to unlock, whereas ad-free models can display your current book cover as the sleep screen and wake directly to your page.

With basic hardware now starting at $149, saving 13% by avoiding lock-screen advertisements feels less acceptable to buyers, especially when competitors like Kobo, Pocketbook and Onyx Boox offer feature-rich alternatives for comparable or better prices.

Amazon launched its Kindle with Special Offers back in 2011. It was a way to spend less when buying a Kindle e-reader for the first time. Kindle director Jay Marine said in an interview at the time that the release of a cheaper, ad-studded Kindle is Amazon’s way of getting the device into the hands of more people. But it also shows Amazon is getting more aggressive in its efforts to lure consumers tempted by competing e-readers and bombarded by ads for Apple iPad and a growing number of competing tablet computers.

What type of ads show up?

Most ads featured on the lock screen are house ads—promotions for books available on the Amazon Kindle Store, upcoming releases, or Amazon services. Occasionally, Amazon may feature external product promotions, but the primary driver is to steer you back toward making digital purchases within its retail network.

If you buy smutty books, these ads might occasionally lead to discovering new authors. However, when you take a Kindle out in public, you might not want these types of books to show up. Manga readers will also be inundated with all sorts of debauched content all over the Kindle. This prompted Amazon to launch an ad filtering system.

Amazon does not sell ad-supported Kindles in Canada because localized promotional campaigns and “Special Offers” infrastructure are primarily built for the larger U.S. retail ecosystem. Delivering localized, relevant book and retail ads requires specific regional marketing pipelines that Amazon has largely kept exclusive to larger markets, such as the U.S. and select European countries.

Wrap Up

I think that Ad-supported Kindles make less sense in 2026 following recent price increases, making the $20 savings less impactful compared to rising hardware costs and stronger competition.

Amazon plans to discount the Kindle e-readers back to their normal prices for the Prime Day Big Deals event in early October. This is the obvious test: if the discounts go deep, the ad tier stops looking quite so exposed.

entries.title: Kobo e-readers receive new software update
entries.summary: Kobo issued new software for its latest e-readers. They solved a lingering payment issue with their online bookstore and are laying the groundwork for Storygraph on older devices. The post Kobo e-readers receive new software update first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Rakuten Kobo e-readers have just received a new firmware update with advent of 4.46 for the Clara Colour, Kobo Clara BW, and Kobo Libra Colour. The main event is a new SSL certificate for the devices to connect to the online bookstore to buy digital content such as audiobooks, e-books, comics, and manga.

Before this new software, the current generation Kobo e-readers had problems paying for digital content on the Rakuten Kobo online bookstore.

Kobo e-readers have had Storygraph pushed out to their devices for a couple of months now. This new software is laying the groundwork to bring the functionality to older devices. This might result in the previous generation getting the social reading platform.

entries.title: New Pocketbook Q is a phone-sized e-reader
entries.summary: Renowned Swiss e-reader brand PocketBook’s latest model is small enough to slip into a pocket and light enough to carry everywhere, putting a library of books and audiobooks within easy reach while leaving the digital distractions of a smartphone behind. The post New Pocketbook Q is a phone-sized e-reader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
PocketBook is launching its Q design e-reader this Fall and will debut it at IFA 2026. The phone-sized e-reader, with a 5.84-inch eye-safe, glare-free E Ink Carta 1300 touchscreen, is designed for everyday reading and listening to audiobooks. Physical side buttons make turning pages effortless with one hand, while the Linux-based platform keeps the experience focused on reading rather than notifications and endless scrolling. The product will be available in late fall for $235.00.

The Pocketbook Q features a 5.84’’ touchscreen display with an E INK Carta 1300 e-paper panel. The resolution is 788 × 1576 with 300 PPI and only has a black-and-white display. Adaptive SMARTlight lets readers adjust both brightness and color temperature, shifting from crisp, cooler tones during the day to warmer ones for evening reading. With the LEDs illuminating the screen rather than shining directly into the eyes, reading stays comfortable even in total darkness. Dark Mode offers even more freedom to choose the most comfortable screen setting, whatever the situation. While IPX4-rated water resistance adds protection for reading on the go

Under the hood is a RockChip RK3566 1.8GHz quad-core processor, 1 GB of RAM, and 32GB of internal storage. There is WIFI to connect to the Pocketbook Bookstore or surf the internet. Listen to audiobooks, podcasts, or music with wireless headphones or earbuds via Bluetooth 5.0. It is powered by a 1550 mAh battery, which should last 3 or 4 weeks with light usage.

PocketBook Q gives readers the freedom to build their library without being tied to a single bookstore or content platform. It supports 25 popular ebook formats without conversion, making it easy to enjoy books, comics, and documents from many different sources. Compatibility with Adobe DRM and LCP DRM allows borrowing ebooks from public libraries, including through the pre-installed PocketBook x Libby app. PocketBook Cloud and the PocketBook Reader mobile app keep books, bookmarks, and reading progress synchronized across devices, so every title is always close at hand. This open approach to reading fits naturally with PocketBook Q’s compact, take-anywhere design.

entries.title: What are E INK Kaleido 3, Gallery 3, and Spectra 6?
entries.summary: Spectra 6, Kaleido 3, and Gallery 3 represent E Ink's top-tier color e-paper display technologies. Each one caters to unique needs, boasting distinct color depths and varying refresh speeds tailored for specific applications. The post What are E INK Kaleido 3, Gallery 3, and Spectra 6? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
E INK has three different types of color e-paper technology that are geared towards different markets and use cases. Kaleido 3 and Gallery 3 are primarily aimed at the e-reader and e-notebook market. Spectra 6 is typically used for digital signage and price tags in grocery stores.

Kaleido 3

Kaleido 3 is the third-generation color electronic paper technology developed by E Ink Holdings, designed to bring color to e-readers and e-note devices while maintaining a paper-like reading experience. It offers richer colors, increasing its color saturation by 30% compared to the previous generation, E Ink Kaleido Plus, in addition to 16 levels of grayscale and 4,096 colors. Kaleido 3 also uses E Ink ComfortGaze, a new front light technology that reduces the amount of blue light, with a reduced Blue Light Ratio (BLR) and Blue Light Toxicity Factor (BLTF) by up to 60% and 24%, respectively. BLR is the ratio of toxic blue to total blue light output, and BLTF is the ratio of brightness to hazardous blue. Additionally, the responsiveness of the ink means that Kaleido 3 can play animations and videos. Adds an RGB (Red, Green, Blue) micro-color filter array on top, producing 4,096 colors at a 150 PPI resolution.

Gallery 3

E Ink Gallery 3 is a full-color electronic paper technology that uses a four-particle ink system (cyan, magenta, yellow, and white) inside every single pixel rather than layering a color filter over a black-and-white screen. E Ink Gallery 3 is based on the E Ink ACeP™ Advanced Color ePaper platform. In this platform, a full-color gamut is achieved through a four-particle ink system: cyan, magenta, yellow, and white, which allows a full color gamut at each pixel.

In Gallery 3, the black and white update time has been improved to 350 milliseconds (ms), the fast color mode is 500 ms, standard color mode is 750-1000 ms, and best color is achieved at 1500 ms. This is a substantial improvement over the first generation of E Ink Gallery, which had a black and white update time of two seconds and color updates of ten seconds. In addition, Gallery 3 will have an improved resolution of 300 pixels per inch (ppi) versus the earlier 150ppi and an operating temperature of 0-50 degrees Celsius, on par with black-and-white eReaders. E Ink Gallery 3 will also support pen input in black and white, with the addition of several other colors and an update time of 30 ms. E Ink Gallery 3 will feature E Ink’s new ComfortGaze™ front light, which offers a blue-light-safe viewing experience.

Spectra 6

E Ink Spectra 6 is a full-color e-paper display technology designed to replace paper signs, digital art frames, and retail displays. Built upon its previous generations, E Ink Spectra 6 offers a better colour spectrum and a highly advanced colour imaging algorithm. Its predecessors, Spectra 3000 and Spectra 3100, introduced a 3-particle (for black, white, and red) and a 4-particle system (for yellow), respectively. In contrast, Spectra 6 has six different colour particles, which can be combined for full-colour images. Offers up to 200 pixels per inch (PPI) with a contrast ratio of around 30:1. It is compatible with E INK Sparkle and supports a partial image flashing effect to add motion for advertising.

entries.title: Lithuania has an e-book piracy issue
entries.summary: E-book piracy in Lithuania is a persistent challenge fueled by a severe shortage of legal electronic books in the Lithuanian language. The post Lithuania has an e-book piracy issue first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Lithuania faces a severe e-book piracy problem, with internet users visiting illegal downloading sites at twice the European Union average. Publishing representatives have warned that the illegal distribution of e-books remains a major but under-discussed problem, with popular titles sometimes appearing on piracy platforms within hours of publication.

A recent study commissioned by Lithuania’s Ministry of Culture in 2024 revealed that 60% of individuals who engaged with written digital content—encompassing ebooks, audiobooks, and online magazines—reported relying solely on legal sources. Additionally, 14% admitted to using a mix of both legal and pirated content, while 5% primarily or exclusively accessed pirated material. Notably, 20% of respondents were uncertain about their sources for such content.

The exact scale of ebook piracy in Lithuania remains difficult to determine because no institution systematically collects such data, said Laura Tekorė, executive director of the Lithuanian Publishers Association. Once a book is released digitally, its further distribution becomes difficult to control, she added. Calculations by Vilnius University researchers Arūnas Gudinavičius and Vincas Grigas showed that between 6,000 and 7,000 Lithuanian-language ebooks were legally available at the end of 2020, while one piracy website alone offered about 5,000 titles.

entries.title: 5 Must-Listen Audiobooks About the Fascinating History of Casinos
entries.summary: Audiobooks suit that history surprisingly well. A good narrator can turn a business dispute or dusty casino opening into something that feels closer to storytelling than a lecture. Here are five worth putting in your listening queue. The post 5 Must-Listen Audiobooks About the Fascinating History of Casinos first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Casinos tend to be remembered through images: neon signs, green felt, crowded tables, sharp suits, and hotel towers glowing in the desert. Yet their history is much richer than the familiar movie version. Behind those bright rooms sit centuries of changing social habits, ambitious business deals, larger-than-life personalities, and plenty of stories that sound almost too strange to be true.

Audiobooks suit that history surprisingly well. A good narrator can turn a business dispute or dusty casino opening into something that feels closer to storytelling than a lecture. Here are five worth putting in your listening queue.

1. Roll the Bones: The History of Gambling — David G. Schwartz

For the big picture, this is probably the best place to start. David G. Schwartz looks beyond Las Vegas and traces gambling across centuries, showing how games of chance became tied to culture, money, politics, and entertainment. The Casino Edition audiobook runs nearly 17 hours and is narrated by Eric Martin.

What makes it work is perspective. Casinos didn’t simply appear under the Nevada sun one day. They grew out of a much older human fascination with risk and chance. That long history also gives useful context to online Topbet, where the casino experience now exists on a screen rather than inside a grand gaming room. The technology changed the setting, but the basic attraction of chance has a very long memory.

It’s a hefty listen, sure, but it rarely feels like homework.

2. Something for Your Money — David G. Schwartz

Schwartz returns with a more focused story in Something for Your Money: A History of Las Vegas Casinos. Its audiobook edition arrived in July 2025, narrated by Eric Jason Martin, and spends more than 11 hours examining the properties and business ideas that helped make Las Vegas America’s best-known casino city.

This one is especially good for listeners curious about the casino as a business. Buildings matter, of course, but so do pricing, entertainment, customer habits, and the personalities making big calls behind closed doors.

That’s where casino history gets fun. A hotel lobby suddenly becomes a business strategy. A restaurant, show, or room rate can tell you something about the audience a casino wanted to attract.

3. Casino: Love and Honor in Las Vegas — Nicholas Pileggi

Need a little more menace in your headphones? Nicholas Pileggi’s Casino brings organized crime into the picture, telling a nonfiction story built around love, betrayal, money, murder, and Mafia power in Las Vegas. The audiobook is narrated by Ken Weitzman.

Pileggi writes with the pace of crime fiction, which explains why the material became so famous beyond the page. Yet underneath the drama sits an important part of casino history: the relationships between operators, powerful outsiders, money, and control.

The result feels less like a museum tour and more like overhearing conversations you probably weren’t supposed to hear.

4. Blood Aces — Doug J. Swanson

Las Vegas history has plenty of oversized characters, and Benny Binion certainly qualifies. Doug J. Swanson’s Blood Aces follows the casino owner whose story became closely tied to the growth of Las Vegas and the creation of the World Series of Poker. John McLain narrates the roughly 11-hour audiobook.

Swanson gives the story some grit. There’s money, ambition, poker, and the restless energy of a city still inventing its identity.

It also shows something easy to forget when looking at modern casino resorts: many famous institutions began with people making bold, messy decisions without knowing what Las Vegas would become.

5. At the Sands — David G. Schwartz

Finish with a bit of old-school glamour. At the Sands focuses on the legendary Las Vegas casino and hotel associated with the city’s classic entertainment era. Eric Jason Martin narrates the nine-hour-plus audiobook, whose story brings names including Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, and Sammy Davis Jr. into the atmosphere.

Here, casino history becomes cultural history. The gaming floor is only part of the attraction. Music, celebrity, nightlife, hospitality, and image all helped build the Las Vegas fantasy people carried home with them.

And perhaps that’s the thread connecting all five books. Casinos have never been only about games. They’re businesses, social spaces, stages, architectural statements, and sometimes crime stories rolled into one. Put on a good pair of headphones, and that history becomes remarkably hard to pause.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.
